Net neutrality was and is very important. The internet is Ma Bell of the modern era. We had a model that worked well. Providers would pay for peering agreements that could accommodate their total customer base. These are the providers that get Netflix and such online. Service providers would pay for peering agreements that could accommodate the amount of bandwidth they intended to resell to their customers. This is the ISP level providers.

Back in the day the issue was getting bandwidth to the household. The cable companies who provided HBO and cinemax and such realized they had unused capacity in their cable lines and could provide bandwidth to households using DOCSIS standards and cable modems. This was not a threat because typical internet usage was email and surfing websites and sending pictures of cats with pancakes on their head. This was a golden era for cable internet providers.

This changed when streaming content became available. Customers now would watch movies online using the same cable that cable companies sold HBO over. Cable companies realize this and began providing their own streaming services. Thus the conflict of interest began. Cable companies employing system administrators pressured those administrators to manage bandwidth so that the company provided streaming services would be favored over content coming from the internet at large. This is a textbook conflict of interest.

Any internet provider must be categorized as a common carrier and subject to governance that keeps common carriers from discriminating based upon origin and destination of traffic. In the mid 1980s when Ma Bell was broken up, a phenomenon was observed and documented whereby telephone calls from Bell to Bell exhibited a high degree of quality but calls from Bell to third-party providers exhibited low quality and frequent drop calls. This was the origin of the common carrier law and this is the same type of phenomena exhibited by current throttling behavior.

Sometimes government regulation is required.
Can you please explain for us non-IT fags what common carrier regulations would entail?

It's a legal framework that carried over from package transport law. Fedex, UPS, USPS, DHL, etc are "common carriers" in that they dont look inside your package and therefor are not legally liable for the contents of your package. If you hand them a 20 kilo box they dont ask or know if it's 20 kilos of yarn or heroin. The technological equivalent of this are ISPs. They dont peak inside your internet usage on their own initiative and arent responsible if you pirate every Jerry Springer episode in history.

Non-common carriers know what's in the box and are responsible for it. E.g. if I hire a secure shipping service to transport a Van Gogh, they'll look in the box, verify what it is, and be liable for what they're shipping.

This needs to be applied to social media websites - either they are common carriers who dont peak in to see what you're doing (and hence arent liable for what you post), or they do peak and are now publishers who are responsible for the content they're curating just like CNN is for their articles.
